## Active

### D-700 — blong-agent: an engine is a framework adapter in blong-gogo

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The SDK client belongs to a base adapter in core/blong-gogo, src/adapter/server/agent.ts, because a
handler may not drive an SDK of its own. Four engine kinds sit behind that one adapter: Vercel AI
SDK, Mastra, DeepSeek Harness and a scripted sim. DeepSeek is driven through the published
@deepseek-ai/dsh-sdk-client, which spawns the dsh runtime over stdio JSON-RPC; the clone at
work/blong/deepseek-harness is the reference for its API and not a vendored dependency. The sim
replays a scripted dialogue so the tests need no network and no key. The harness is alpha and its
client a release candidate, so each kind is imported dynamically and a missing package fails one
account rather than the process. The methods stay three segments on the adapter's own namespace:
engine.step.run, engine.session.run, engine.session.close and engine.account.check.

### D-702 — blong-agent: a late answer is a database row, not a promise

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The hot path is blong-chat's parked promise, awaited with a thirty minute timeout passed as
timeoutMs. An answer that arrives after that promise is gone, or on a pod that does not hold the
workspace, must be forwarded by blong-chat to agent.answer.receive, which writes an agent_answer row
keyed by the prompt id. The worker that owns the session consumes the row and resumes from the
checkpoint, and a repeated delivery is idempotent on the prompt id. A broker may also wake that
worker the moment the row lands, but the row is the record and the tick poll is the fallback
(@@D-709). This needs one change in realm/blong-chat: an answer nobody is waiting for must honour
the configured forward instead of being acknowledged and dropped.

### D-704 — blong-agent: the worker is a group on the dispatch orchestrator

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The background loop hangs off the realm's own dispatch orchestrator, orchestrator/agentDispatch.ts:
a worker group exposes agent.worker.tick, and the orchestrator's start opens an unref'd interval
behind an in-flight guard while stop clears it. Keeping the worker on the same orchestrator as the
methods it calls is what lets the loop reach them without a broker, and exposing the cycle as a
method is what lets a test drive exactly one claim and run without waiting on a timer. A cron
schedule cannot hold the awaiting call the hot path needs, and it cannot stop a second pass from
overlapping the first.

### D-705 — blong-agent: a recovered session asks the channel before it writes

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A boot janitor scans only the workspace directory of its own host and matches it against sessions
whose lease has expired. A match is not resumed silently: the channel is asked to confirm, because a
crash may have interrupted a write. Confirmation resumes from the latest checkpoint, a refusal
purges the directory and fails the ticket, and no answer leaves the session suspended for the next
boot rather than destroying work nobody judged. The same confirmation covers a repeat ticket, so a
resumed session states what it is about to do before it edits anything.

### D-707 — blong-agent: the ticket is an adapter; fixtures now, blong-task later

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The pool belongs to a realm that does not exist yet: blong-task will own tickets, claim and lease,
so blong-agent holds no agent_ticket table. The agent reaches the pool through a task adapter whose
first implementation is a fixture list in the realm, seeded from YAML, exposing nextClaim, release
and edit; the worker's ownership rule lives on the agent's own session row, which records the worker
that holds the workspace. When blong-task lands it replaces that one adapter's implementation, and
the loop does not change.

### D-708 — blong-agent: a session names its engine mode, step or native loop

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

DeepSeek Harness runs its own agent loop; the SDK client spawns the dsh runtime and a prompt returns
when the whole agent is idle. An adapter that insisted on one turn would fight that, so a session
records its mode: step, where the realm owns the loop and the adapter returns tool calls, or native,
where the engine owns the loop and reports its events. Both write the neutral transcript to a
checkpoint, and a native session also stores the engine session id, which is what resumeSession
needs after a restart. Vercel, Mastra and the simulator are step engines; DeepSeek is native.

### D-709 — blong-agent: a broker wakes the owner, the answer row is the truth

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A broker is a wake-up, never the record: the answer is a row first, and a notification carrying the
session and prompt id tells the owning pod to look now instead of on its next tick. The notify
adapter has a redis implementation and a kafka one, chosen by configuration, kafka using a unique
consumer group per pod so every pod sees every message, and the tick poll remains the fallback that
makes a lost notification harmless. This keeps correctness in the database and latency in the
broker.

### D-710 — blong-agent: the agent may run commands; the container is the boundary

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The agent runs commands in its workspace, because a coding agent that cannot build or test is not
one. The boundary is the container rather than a command allowlist: execFile with an argv array and
no shell, the ticket directory as cwd, a wall-clock timeout, an output cap, a scrubbed environment
that carries no secrets, and one event row per command. The capability is switchable per deployment,
and the deployment runs it on a pod that mounts only the workspace volume.

### D-711 — blong-agent: a native engine brings its own tools, the realm brings the human

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

DeepSeek Harness ships fs, shell and sandbox tools and runs them itself, so a native session already
reads, writes and runs commands with the ticket directory as its root; the harness enforces the
boundary the workspace adapter enforces for a step engine. Registering the realm's own tools with it
would mean serving MCP from the realm, a second protocol with no new capability, so that is a later
decision. What the realm must supply is the human: the client's onUserQuestion answers an ask and
onRequest handles an approval request, and both route to the same question handler the step path
uses. A native account therefore differs from a step account in who owns the tool loop and which
tools run, not in how a person is asked.

### D-712 — blong-agent: an adapter owns its namespace and may be instanced twice

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

An adapter instance owns its namespace, and one base adapter may be instantiated more than once in a
process, which is what chat already does with slack and viber both extending adapter.webhook.
Methods are therefore named after the namespace and not after the realm: engine.step.run belongs to
the engine instance of adapter.agent, and a second instance named review answers review.step.run
with its own account map. The consequence for this realm is that a session must record the instance
it ran on as well as the account inside it, because the same alias may exist in both and a resume
that guessed the wrong instance would reach the wrong endpoint.

### D-717 — A k8s contribution belongs in the default activation block, not release

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A k8s tree is generated by a k8s run, which merges the default block and nothing else, so a
contribution declared under release is invisible to the generator and the tree comes out without the
volume, the Secret reference or the sizing. The division that works is: the k8s keys live in
default, where only the generator reads them, and anything that must differ between a checkout and a
deployment (the workspace root, which names the directory a claim is mounted at) lives in release,
where the deployment's value belongs. A realm that puts both in release gets a tree that silently
lacks its resources; one that puts both in default gets a checkout writing to a cluster path.

### D-724 — A persona is an agent row that names an account, never a secret

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A persona collects everything one needs to work: engine mode, model, parameters, allowed tools, step
and call ceilings, instructions, workspace mode and the continuation window. Credentials stay in the
account map, because a persona that carried `baseUrl` and `apiKeyEnv` would put secrets in two
places and the k8s env contribution is generated from accounts already. Resolution is persona over
account over the provider defaults from `agentProvider`, so a persona that names no account inherits
the realm default.

### D-726 — Persona presets are config, materialised by a production seed

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The first personas are declared under `agent.persona.presets` and written to the table by
`agentPersonaPresetMerge`, which `meta/db/agentPersonaPresetMerge.yaml` dispatches on every start.
The merge inserts only what is absent, so a row edited later survives a restart, and an explicit
overwrite flag is what re-applies a changed preset. This is the shape an admin UI writes later, so
the UI adds rows rather than replacing a code path.

### D-728 — Summarising is the default compaction level, and the realm implements it

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Summarising is the default level and the only one this realm implements itself, because it is the
only level that works for every persona: a toolless persona has no workspace for a restart to
commit, and pruning alone does not keep a long conversation inside the window. At a threshold the
realm asks a model to condense the transcript up to the last kept turns, writes the next checkpoint
with that summary at its head in place of the turns it replaced, and counts the crossing on the
session, so a resume, a prune and the stats command all see the compacted transcript and no handler
has to know a summary exists. The cost is one model turn per crossing, which is why the threshold
sits well below the window and the persona may name a cheaper model for the summary. The threshold
is estimated locally from the transcript until the engine reports usage (@@T-594), and the three
engine-native routes stay unused because each is tied to one engine, one dependency or one harness
home.

### D-729 — A chat turn appends to the conversation session it continues

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A message continues the session its channel was last active in, while that activity is inside the
persona continuation window: the turn appends a user message to the latest checkpoint and runs from
there, because a run only reads its opening prompt when the transcript is empty. A spent turn leaves
the session done, and done is still continuable; only a window that has passed, or the new command,
closes it. A chat session carries its channel key as its ticket id and an empty workspace path,
because those two columns predate chat sessions and the schema sync adds columns rather than
relaxing them. The persona picker uses an id derived from the channel, so a caller can answer it
without having been told the id, and the consumer reads the channel row back when its caller did not
attach one, because writing a binding and reading it must not need two different callers.

### D-933 — The agent records which loop drove a session and whether a tick claimed

> _2026-11-20 · realm/blong-agent · active_

`realm/blong-agent` declares two decisions and records them: `agentEngineMode` (which loop drives a
session — `native`, where the engine owns its own loop, or `step`, where the realm drives one turn,
its calls and a checkpoint at a time) and `agentClaim` (whether a tick takes a ticket — `claim`, or
`noAccount` when nothing could run what it took). Both are declared in `lukaot/signal.ts`, so the
arms are a closed set the compiler checks (`@@D-914`), and each is announced by a record beside it:
`agentSessionEngineChosen` at `info`, and `agentTicketClaimed` at `info` or `agentWorkerIdle` at
`warn`.

The rule this cost a cycle to learn: a decision's rationale belongs to
the **next record in the scope**, so `decide` is called immediately before the line that states its
consequence, never once at the top of a handler whose next step is an `await` over the pool — the
records that await writes would take the rationale away from the line that says what was decided.
The tick therefore calls a small `decideClaim()` beside each announcement rather than deciding once.
A signal at `debug` is a rationale nobody reads: the mode line is `info` for that reason.

`test/lukaot.reach.test.ts` asserts both on the records themselves: the claim carries
`decision.discriminator = 'agentClaim'`, its chosen arm, and the intent of the execution it served;
the session's mode line carries `agentEngineMode`. Sport's `sportGenderDerived` was moved onto the
same form — declared, with camelCase arms (`oneGender`) — because a bare string decision is accepted
but its arms are never validated.

### D-706 — blong-agent: the realm is realm/blong-agent, the blueprint is core/blong-agent

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Two folders would otherwise share the name. core/blong-agent is an evaluation blueprint with no
package manifest, and the new realm is the package feasibleone blong-agent under realm/blong-agent.
The blueprint is worth adopting as a test inside the realm later, because it is the only measure of
how well the instructions produce a realm, and that adoption is explicitly out of scope for this
plan. Until someone does it, a path beginning with core/blong-agent means the blueprint and never
the realm.

### D-972 — One account per runtime host, not a pool inside one account

> _2026-11-23 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#300](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/300).

`agent_session.engineAccount` already pins the session to one account, and a resume must reach the
runtime that holds the session — so the pin has to be the host. `srv1` and `srv2` are two accounts
with one runtime each; `local` is a third, for a runtime started by hand on the developer host. The
realm runs in the dev cluster, so every account is reached over the network and none of them is a
co-located runtime. Choosing between `srv1` and `srv2` is the task adapter's job, later.

### D-974 — The realm's file and shell tools are not offered to a copilot session

> _2026-11-23 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#300](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/300).

The harness edits files and runs commands on the runtime host. Registering `readFile` beside the
runtime's own `edit_file` would be two filesystems in one transcript, and the realm's tools would
act on the realm's `workspace.root`, not on the directory the agent sees. A copilot account declares
the tool names it can serve (`askHuman`, `finish`), and the realm filters with that list.

### D-976 — A native session parks by aborting its run, and resumes on a user turn

> _2026-11-23 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#300](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/300).

A tool result cannot be handed to a process that has gone; the harness keeps its own transcript, so
the answer is delivered as the next user message and the engine folds it in with everything else it
remembers. `IAgentSessionResult` reports `suspended` with the prompt id, the realm records the
suspension exactly as it does for a step engine, and the engine session id is kept.

### D-980 — A native engine's command switch is a realm setting, because the adapter's never sees it

> _2026-11-23 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The harness runs its own shell, so workspace.shell.enabled on the workspace adapter never sees the
command. The realm carries agent.agentDispatch.shellEnabled (default true) and hands it to the
engine as allowShell. Measured against runtime 1.0.114, a coding-agent session does not consult
permissions.onRequest for the shell: echo hi ran in manual mode without a single permission request,
so a switch enforced only there was documented but not real. The switch is therefore the runtime's
own shell tools excluded from the session (bash, powershell, shell), and the permission handler
stays as a second line for a runtime that does ask. The cost is that a deployment disables two keys
instead of one; the alternative was a native engine silently bypassing the switch, which is worse.

### D-978 — A copilot workspace lives on the runtime host and the realm never prepares it

> _2026-11-23 · realm/blong-agent · active_

An account names workspaceRoot, the working folder the servers keep, and a claim records it as the
session's workspace instead of running workspace.repo.prepare. The folder is the workspace rather
than a per-ticket subdirectory because the runtime refuses a session whose workingDirectory does not
exist, and nothing on the realm's side can create a directory on the runtime host: measured against
runtime 1.0.114, session.create fails with 'Directory does not exist or cannot be accessed', and the
SDK's file fetch requires the parent to exist already. One worker per runtime host is what makes one
folder enough, and the agent clones, pulls and pushes the repository in it with the harness's own
tools, so the servers carry a git credential and trust the folder. A workspaceKind on agent_session
marks the path remote, because the recovery janitor must never hand a server's directory to the
local workspace adapter. A per-ticket directory comes back when something on the host can create
one.

### D-984 — blong-agent publishes engine.account.check on its gateway

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The engine adapter answers `engineAccountCheck` in `core/blong-gogo`, and the deployment docs told
an operator to call it by hand, but a gateway serves only the methods its own layer validates: the
method existed in the process and nowhere a caller could reach. The realm now carries
`gateway/engine/engine.account.check.ts`, a validation-only file beside the `agent.*` routes — the
implementation stays in the adapter, the gateway layer declares params and result, and the default
`jwt` auth is also what makes the MLE hook decode an encrypted body on that path. It is the first
route here whose subject is a framework adapter namespace rather than the realm's own, so the folder
is `gateway/engine/` and the method keeps the three segments `D-700` gives it.

### D-985 — The provisioning script takes its secrets from the environment file, not the command line

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

copilot-runtime.sh is run as root, so the obvious invocation is `sudo GH_TOKEN=... bash ...`. It
works — Ubuntu's default `%sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL` implies the `SETENV` tag, so the assignment
reaches the script — but sudo parses the assignment out of its own argument list and then waits for
the script, so `/proc/<sudo-pid>/cmdline` (world-readable, and printed by `ps aux`) carries the
token for the whole install, and the typed line is in the operator's shell history for good. The
script already reads `GH_TOKEN` and `COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY` out of
`/etc/blong/copilot-worker.env` before rewriting it, so the documented flow seeds that file (0600
root) and passes nothing: rotation is an edited line and a re-run. The environment-variable form
stays accepted and is documented as the loud one; the earlier README recommended it, which is what
put two PATs and two provider keys in an install script and a history file.

### D-987 — Telemetry is one Kafka topic keyed by session id, and the session row remembers its partition

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#307](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/307).

One topic avoids a topic per ticket (metadata, ACLs, retention per topic) while the key keeps a
session's events on one partition in order. The partition is learned once, from the delivery report
of the first event, and stored on `agent.session`, so a reader never hashes anything and two readers
agree.

### D-991 — The session UI is the agent realm's own browser platform, and its heavy parts load per page

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#307](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/307).

Putting agent UI into `core/blong-browser` ships it to every portal, including those that never run
an agent; putting it into another realm splits one feature across two packages. The realm mirrors
what `realm/blong-viewer` does — `browser.ts` globbing `browser/**`, a `portalConfigGet` menu group,
and a `component` handler whose `component: async () => import(...)` is the page (`viewer.log` is
the worked example). That import is what keeps markdown, mermaid and the highlighter in a chunk of
their own: the portal shell never loads them, and neither does a person who never opens the tab.

### D-992 — History is what Kafka retains; MySQL carries the projection

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#307](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/307).

Kafka holds the deltas for the topic's retention (7–30 days, deployment's choice) and is the only
complete record. MySQL keeps what a list and a header need without replaying a topic: the session
row, its partition, and a summary written by a projector consumer (turns, tokens, per-tool counts
and durations, last activity). A session older than retention renders its summary and says the
detail expired, which is the "old messages omit details" requirement.

### D-993 — `agent.event` stays the resume trace and is not the UI's source

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Planned in [#307](https://github.com/feasibleone/blong/issues/307).

The resume path reads it to know what a session did before a checkpoint; it truncates payloads on
purpose. Feeding the UI from it would turn one store into two purposes and reintroduce the
truncation the page exists to avoid. The UI reads the stream; the resume reads the table.

### D-1004 — The projector folds a batch at insert, not from a second consumer

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The projection runs inside `agent.telemetry.insert`, over the batch it just published, rather than
in a consumer of the topic. The plan called for a consumer that commits offsets; what the summary
needs is the events, and they are already in the process that reports them, so a second group member
on the feed would re-read what was just written and add a broker round trip to every deployment for
nothing. The reducer stays pure (`agentMetricProject`), so a consumer can be added the day a second
process must project events it did not publish — and the row it writes is already the shape that
consumer would upsert.

### D-1005 — The memory source lives in the realm until a second realm needs one

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The memory ring a Playwright run watches is the realm's own module rather than a framework adapter,
which is what the plan asked for. Only this realm publishes a feed today, so a framework adapter
would be an abstraction with one implementation and a config key no other realm sets; the ring keeps
the contract the route needs (a tail, a cursor, a live sequence) inside `orchestrator/session/`.
When a second realm wants a memory source the module moves beside the Kafka adapter and both become
sources of one contract — the plan's own words, deferred until there is a second caller.

### D-1007 — The session list pages by a tie-broken cursor, because updatedAt is second-precision

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The projection's timestamps are MySQL `datetime`, which keeps whole seconds, so `agent.session.find`
ordering by `updatedAt` alone ties every row written in the same second and a keyset page that asks
for `updatedAt < cursor` silently drops the rest of that second. The route therefore orders by
`updatedAt desc, sessionId desc` and its `next` cursor is `<iso>|<sessionId>`, which the handler
reads back as a pair: the bare timestamp still pages a caller that passes one, and the pair is what
a page list hands back. The session id is the tiebreaker because it is the primary key and therefore
total - any monotonic column would do the same, but one already exists.

### D-1008 — The page takes no test seam; a scripted browser run needs the memory source behind the same route

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The page reads `agent.session.find` and `agent.session.watch` through the handler proxy, so a
browser test needs a _server_ that answers both with a scripted conversation. The cheap seam would
be a fixture the page reads from `globalThis` when the gateway is absent, and it was rejected: a
production page that branches on a test global is a page whose tested path is not the path a
deployment runs. The alternative costs one server-side change - `agent.session.watch` choosing the
memory ring when `telemetry.source` is `memory` (`@@D-988`), and the ring being fed by the engine's
telemetry dispatch, which is what `T-795`'s ring was built for - and then the spec drives a `sim`
turn the way `test.agent.session` does. That is the shape the remaining browser work takes: the
source is chosen by configuration, never by the test.

### D-1009 — The transcript draws its own chat surface rather than adopting a chat kit

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The page draws its own transcript: a status bar of chips and numbers, and a column of events in
which a message is prose, a reasoning block is a folded one-liner, a run of tool calls is one card
that opens to a row per call, and a state the session is waiting on is a callout. CopilotKit and
assistant-ui were both considered and not taken. Neither knows the shape this realm already reduces
its events into: they bring their own message and tool-call model and their own store, so the
adapter between `telemetryRing`/Kafka frames and their model would be a second definition of a
section — exactly what `sessionSections.ts` is for. They are also built to own the composer and the
assistant loop, which this page does not have: a session is opened and read, not typed into. What
the ready components would have given cheaply is the look, and that is CSS over the same markup; the
dependency is the expensive half.

The body above first said CopilotKit needs a runtime the deployment would host. That was wrong, and
reading `CopilotChatMessageView`'s reference page corrected it: the message view is presentational,
takes `messages` and `isRunning`, and requires no provider — the runtime belongs to the
chat-completion side, which this page does not have. The decision stands on the model mismatch
rather than on a hosted runtime, and the concepts the view documents were taken instead of the
component (`@@D-1010`). If a composer ever lands — a person steering a running session — the
calculus changes, and assistant-ui's primitives fit a React 19 page better than CopilotKit's runtime
does.

### D-1010 — The transcript borrows CopilotKit's message-view concepts without the component

> _2026-11-24 · realm/blong-agent · active_

`CopilotChatMessageView`'s reference page was read as a design source, and five of its concepts
shape the transcript although the component is not used (`@@D-1009`). Its roles are vocabulary, not
a model: `user | assistant | reasoning | activity`, so every section carries `data-role` and a
stylesheet can address a kind of turn without knowing which reduction produced it, and a run of tool
calls is one `activity` row instead of one box per call. Its cursor is the statement that a run in
progress is drawn once, at the end, and hidden when the last message is itself reasoning — reasoning
is the visible sign of work, so a mark beside it says the same thing twice; the page does the same
with `.agent-cursor`, keyed on the stream's running state and suppressed after a reasoning section.
Its `isLatest` is passed to the last row only, so a stylesheet can distinguish the message someone
is reading from the ones above it. Its grouped tool-call mode is the answer to a wall of
near-identical cards: a run of two or more calls folds to `Used 3 tools · bash ×2, edit`, and
opening the row gives one line per call, each opening to its arguments and output —
`toolGrouping.ts` folds the sections and `sessionRowsOf` is what the page loops over. Its interrupt
placement is the callout: the human-in-the-loop element is drawn after the messages rather than
inline, because it is what the run stopped on and not part of the work it did.

Not taken yet, each a lead rather than a gap: past fifty rows the reference virtualises, which would
matter for a long session and not yet for a seeded one; it renders a `user` turn from the ticket,
whereas this page shows the question only in an `awaiting` note, so a session whose ticket title is
not the prompt has nothing to render as the person's words; its work summary excludes time spent
waiting for approval, which is a more honest duration than summing calls; its slot system (a
component, a class name or partial props per slot) is how a host realm would restyle the view
without forking it, and is the right shape if this page is ever contributed by more than one realm;
and `transformMessages`/`groupMessages` are the seam a migration would hang on — a mapping from
`ISessionSection` to their message shape, kept in one module, which is what makes a later move to
the component a dependency swap rather than a rewrite. The reference's per-call display modes
(`grouped | line | stacked | turn | separate`) are also worth revisiting when a session runs more
than one kind of tool per turn: `grouped` is what this page does, and `stacked` may read better when
tool names repeat.

### D-1011 — The transcript colours code with a grammar library rather than a scanner of its own

> _2026-11-25 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The page carried a hand-written scanner for bash, TypeScript, JSON, CSS and HTML (`@@T-799`), and it
coloured everything else flat — which stopped being acceptable as soon as an engine wrote Python,
YAML or a diff. `@speed-highlight/core` v2 is taken instead: ~1.5 kB of core, a few hundred bytes
per grammar, no dependencies, and its `tokenizeWith` is synchronous with the grammars passed by the
caller, so nothing is loaded on demand and a fence never renders flat for a frame while its grammar
arrives. Sugar High was the alternative the research named, and the size it quoted (~1.7 kB) is v1's
core: its own benchmark puts the TypeScript bundle at 5.16 KiB gzip, and its `highlight` returns an
HTML string. Speed-highlight is smaller, faster in both its own and the competitor's measurement,
and its callback hands `(text, type)` back, so the page keeps building spans rather than setting
`innerHTML` — a fence that contains markup stays text, which a unit test now pins. MicroLighter is
not taken: it needs post-mount DOM ranges, and this page re-renders on every streamed delta.

Two consequences are part of the decision rather than details of it. The whole fence is tokenized in
one call and then cut at the newlines the token stream carries, because a page that coloured each
line alone broke every comment or template literal that spans two — the renderer had to stop
highlighting per line for the highlighter to be right. And the grammars come from the package's
registry rather than one subpath per language, because a pattern subpath in its exports map does not
resolve under this repo's test loader (`@@F-838`); the registry is all 34 grammars, ~9 kB gzipped,
which is what one import and no second render cost. The palette is now two sets of `--tok-*` custom
properties selected by the portal's `.blong-app-dark` class, because the GitHub-light colours the
page had were unreadable on the dark palette's own code background.

### D-1015 — The answer wake's subscription belongs to the dispatch orchestrator

> _2026-11-25 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The answer wake's subscription is the dispatch orchestrator's: `orchestrator/agentDispatch.ts` opens
`notify.sub.watch` in its `ready()` and dispatches `agent.answer.wake` for each message, and
`adapter/notify/notifyAnswerWake.ts` is gone. Two details were forced. It is `ready()` and not
`start()` because the subscription is opened through another port, and a port registers itself while
it starts, so a call made from `start()` can find nothing to answer it — `ready()` is the phase the
loader runs after every port has started. And the adapter needed a subscription that does not
dispatch: `redis.sub.watch` answers an async iterable of `{channel, message}`, parses nothing and
knows nothing about wakes, so the channel is a sequence its caller reads, the way
`kafka.topic.watch` already was. The channel and the method are orchestrator settings
(`wake.channel`, `wake.method`), defaulting to empty and `agent.answer.wake` and set by the `notify`
activation alone: a deployment with no broker subscribes to nothing and `agentAnswerReceive`
publishes nothing, rather than dispatching at an adapter that was never loaded. A subscription that
cannot be opened is `agentAnswerWakeUnsubscribed`, a warning and never a failure, because the answer
row is still the truth and the tick still finds it.

### D-1017 — The agent deployment takes the chat deployment's place and keeps its hosts and its data

> _2026-11-25 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The chat deployment's place is taken by this realm rather than by a second deployment beside it, and
the tenant's two addresses stay where they are: `chat.feasible.one` for the portal and
`chat-hook.feasible.one` for the Slack and Viber paths. A host is a DNS record, a certificate and a
Slack app's request URL that somebody owns; moving which process answers it is not a reason to move
any of them, and the tree already takes every host from the CR (`@@D-800`), so only the CR's suite
names change.

The data is the chat deployment's, dumped and restored under `blong-agent` before the first
converge, and the migration Job then adds the agent schema beside the chat tables rather than
replacing them — the account rows and the channel memory are the thing nobody wants to set up twice.
The database's name is the source's, while the tenant's rc carries the credentials, which is the
split `@@D-857` already makes for every deployment.

The chat realm stays a child of this entry and a runtime dependency rather than a devDependency, so
`chat.*` keeps answering on the same host and the artifact carries it: a call a developer's machine
makes to `https://chat.feasible.one` and a Slack message that asks an agent a question reach the
same dispatch, which is also the seam a future Slack trigger would use to start a ticket. What is
not carried over is the chat _deployment_: its CR is deleted once the new portal answers, and its
tree, scenario and release entry stay in the repository until somebody decides they are not needed
(`@@T-829`).

### D-1040 — The telemetry topic is provisioned, never created by the handler

> _2026-11-28 · realm/blong-agent · active_

`agent.telemetry.insert` used to create its topic — one idempotent `kafka.topic.create` per process,
remembered in a promise — as a second door beside the declaration in `meta/kafka/telemetry.yaml`.
The door was removed: the base adapter's per-intent blocks already provision the declaration (`dev`
and `integration` best-effort, `upgrade` refusing to continue without it, `@@D-1001`), so the only
runs the create could still help were the ones whose provisioning _should_ have failed — a `release`
process whose `upgrade` Job never ran, or never reached the broker. In those, a create here repaired
the omission silently: the first batch published, nobody learned the step was missing, and the
deployment looked healthy until the retention or the partition count differed from the declaration.
Measured after the removal: deleting `kalin.blong.agent.telemetry` and starting the realm brings it
back from the declaration alone, so the door was also redundant in the ordinary case. A broker with
no such topic now costs the batch its two-second send timeout and reports it as `sourceUnavailable`,
which is the loud version of the same fact (`@@D-988`). This amends the clause of `@@D-1013` that
listed "creates the topic" among the orchestrator's steps.

### D-1013 — An adapter reaches one system, so the telemetry handlers are orchestrators

> _2026-11-25 · realm/blong-agent · active_

`agent.telemetry.insert` and `agent.session.watch` were written in `adapter/db/` because a method
the gateway or the engine reaches by name had to be one the `db` port answered (`@@F-833`). Both are
orchestrations: the first reads the deployment's choice of sink, creates the topic, produces to the
broker or appends to the ring, records the partition on the session row and folds the batch into its
metric; the second chooses between the topic and the ring, computes a tail, and frames records into
a cursor protocol. Written as adapters they reached the `kafka` adapter and the `db` adapter for the
next step — an adapter calling an adapter — and they imported the ring and the projection out of
`orchestrator/session/`, so the dependency ran upward as well. They now live in
`orchestrator/session/` and answer on the dispatch orchestrator instead of being forwarded to `db`,
calling their adapters the way the layer rule intends: `agent.session.get` is answered by the `db`
adapter, so the adapter is named (`db/agentSessionGet`) because its subject is the realm's namespace
and not the adapter's, while `kafkaMessageSend` and `kafkaTopicWatch` need no prefix at all — their
subject already is the `kafka` adapter's own namespace. The wire names, the frames and the stored
documents are unchanged, and `index.test.ts`, `test.agent.feed` and the Playwright spec pass without
an edit.

The rule the change follows, now stated in the adapter and orchestrator pages: an adapter reaches
one system, so it neither calls an orchestrator nor another adapter, and a handler that reads one
system, asks a second and writes a third is an orchestrator wherever it was filed. The wake was the
last such edge and it is gone too: the subscription now lives in the orchestrator that decides what
a message means (`@@T-816`), so an adapter that forwards a delivered event is the exception a
transport may force rather than a shape this realm uses. What still crosses freely is a type, which
is why `agentSessionMetricEdit` may name the orchestrator's `IAgentSessionMetric` without joining
its call graph. Repo-wide there is no other adapter→orchestrator import; `blong-access` has four
qualified calls, all of them `db/*` from inside the `db` group, which is one component using its own
handlers.

One clause above is now history: the insert no longer creates its topic. The declaration in
`meta/kafka/telemetry.yaml` and the base adapter's per-intent blocks are the only door, so a missing
topic is a provisioning failure that reports itself instead of one the first batch repairs
(`@@D-1040`). Everything else here — the placement of the two handlers, and why an adapter may not
call an adapter — stands.

## Superseded

### D-699 — blong-agent: the engine port is one model turn, not one agent run

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · superseded_

Adapters implement a single model turn: they receive the neutral transcript and the tool definitions
and return assistant text and tool calls, executing nothing themselves. The realm owns the loop, so
the transcript it checkpoints is engine-neutral and a session can change engine, or resume on
another host, by replaying that transcript. This is the only shape that makes DeepSeek Harness
resumable, because a Cordis context lives in RAM and cannot be serialised. The cost is that every
turn re-sends the transcript, and a runaway loop is bounded by an explicit step limit rather than by
the SDK.

the one-turn contract is the step mode; a native engine keeps its own loop

Superseded by `D-708`.

### D-701 — blong-agent: the realm owns the ticket pool and leases it in the database

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · superseded_

Tickets are rows in agent_ticket, claimed with one conditional update that sets workerId and
leaseExpiresAt, so two workers cannot take the same ticket and a dead worker's lease expires on its
own. A claim is refused when the ticket names a workspace that does not exist on this host, because
the only process that may touch those files is the one holding the volume. No broker is involved in
the first pass: the database is both the pool and the lease record.

the pool is blong-task's; agent reaches it through a fixture task port

Superseded by `D-707`.

### D-703 — blong-agent: the workspace is a per-ticket git-rollback directory

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · superseded_

A ticket gets workspaceRoot slash ticketId, created from a configured template and recorded with the
base commit it started from. Every tool resolves its path inside that directory and refuses an
escape, because a model writing a parent path is the ordinary case rather than the attack. Rollback
is git checkout plus git clean inside that directory, and the agent executes no shell command in the
first pass: a build or test tool is a later capability that needs its own decision.

the shell is allowed inside the container boundary

Superseded by `D-710`.
